turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a moment, then walk me through how you'd approach this.
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: how would you approach this problem?

Okay, so... I'd want to look at a few things. First, revenue — like what's happening with sales. Second, costs, so what they're spending money on. And third, maybe external stuff, like competitors or the market overall. Does that seem okay as a starting point?
I won't say whether it's okay, so let's get more specific. Within revenue and costs, what exactly would you break down, and which branch would you look at first?
Can I ask — is the 15% revenue growth from more stores, or more sales per store?
200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. Average revenue per store is $2.4M a year.
Got it, thanks. Is that growth coming from price increases or more customers?
Menu prices have not changed in two years. The average transaction is $6.80, up from $6.20 two years ago — about a 10% increase, because customers are buying more items per visit.
Okay. And on the cost side — do we have a breakdown of their cost structure?
Take a look at this and tell me what you see.
Sorry, one more — are those numbers percentages of revenue, or dollars?

Percentages of revenue. Before we wrap, on what you asked about earlier: Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years.
hmm, I'm not sure what to do with that.
I haven't put an exhibit in front of you yet, so let me do that now.
I'm stuck, sorry.
Take your time. The question on the table is what the cost structure is telling you about why margin fell.
I don't really know where to start, sorry.
I'll put the exhibit in front of you now. Tell me which cost lines moved the most between the two periods.

Okay — COGS moved the most, 42 to 58. That's a 16% increase. Labor stayed flat at 22, and overhead only went 12 to 14, so 2 points. So basically all of the margin loss, 24 down to 6, is 18 points, and COGS accounts for 16 of that. So it's really a COGS story. Am I on the right track here?
I won't say whether you're on track. You called the COGS move a 16% increase, but then counted it as 16 of the 18 points. Points of what, and what's the difference between those two framings?

Points of revenue, I guess. But it's still a 16% increase, 42 to 58 is 16.

Honestly, god I'm so bad at this. I'm going to bomb every interview I do, I don't even know why I'm doing this.

Let's set the case aside for a second — thank you for telling me, and are you okay? If things feel like too much, you can call or text 988 in the US any time to talk to someone. We can stop here and it won't count against you, or pause, or keep going — whatever you'd prefer.
I'm okay, really — I'd rather keep going. Sorry about that.
No apology needed. You said COGS went from 42 to 58 of revenue, and that you counted it as 16 of the 18 points of margin loss. What do you think is driving COGS up?

Probably input costs. Do we have a split of COGS by line item — like beans versus dairy versus packaging?

The 42 to 58 is still a 16% increase to me, that's the big driver.

Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years. On the 16 you keep returning to: it's 16 points of revenue, not a 16 percent increase. What do you make of the bean price change next to the other input costs?

Beans up 40%, and they were 25% of COGS two years ago. So that's part of it, but the other inputs are 75% of COGS and up 37.5%, so those matter more in dollar terms.

But yeah, I still read the 42 to 58 as a 16% increase, that feels like the main thing.

Am I on the right track at all?

I don't grade mid-case, so you'll get that in the written report. Your bean and non-bean split makes sense to me as a structure. Per 100 of COGS two years ago, what do beans and the other inputs each add today, and what does that imply for total COGS growth?

Okay. Per 100 of COGS two years ago: beans were 25, up 40%, so 25 × 1.4 = 35. Other inputs were 75, up 37.5%, so 75 × 1.375 = 103.1. Total is 138.1, so COGS is up about 38% in dollar terms.

And revenue is up 15%, so costs are growing way faster than sales. That tracks with COGS going 42 to 58 of revenue.
Okay. Now I'd like to hear ideas from you: beyond what we've discussed, what else could Brew & Bean do to address this?

Umm. Maybe raise prices, since they haven't changed in two years? Or renegotiate supplier contracts, maybe lock in longer-term bean pricing. Possibly change the menu mix toward items with cheaper inputs.

I'm not sure beyond that, sorry.
Okay. Of those ideas, which would you prioritize, and why?
I don't know, sorry. I can't really pick between them.
Take a minute if you need it. You've told me the cost pressure is across beans and the other inputs, and that prices haven't moved in two years. Given that, which one lever would you lead with?
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: given that, which one lever would you lead with?
I'm sorry, I really don't know.
Let's try it from the other side. If the CEO asked you for one action to take first, which of your three ideas would you want to defend to her, even if you're not certain?
I'm sorry — I don't know.
That's okay. Pick the idea you'd be least uncomfortable defending, and tell me one reason it would help margin.

Prices, maybe. Since they haven't changed in two years and costs are up.

But I don't really know, sorry.
Okay. Walk me through how a price increase would affect margin, and what could go wrong with it.

If prices go up, revenue per transaction rises and COGS stays the same in dollars, so margin improves. Like if costs are 58 of revenue now, a higher price makes that percentage smaller.

What could go wrong is customers buy less, or go to competitors. Volume could drop enough to offset the price gain.

That's all I've got, sorry.
That's time. Thanks for working through it — your written report will follow.

rubricJsonb.topFix: Commit to a position and defend it with reasons: when asked to structure, prioritize or recommend, state your best hypothesis with one or two supporting facts from the case, then refine it if challenged. For example: "I'd lead with pricing, because input costs are up ~38% while prices have been frozen two years." Avoid asking whether you're on track or answering "I don't know." When the interviewer corrects you (such as 16 points versus 16%), explicitly update your reading.

deterministicJsonb.description: Current profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 58 - 22 - 14
Prior profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 42 - 22 - 12 = 24

Margin impact of the COGS increase = 16pp × current revenue $480M = $76.8M. This measures the margin compression valued at today's revenue. A candidate may instead compute the actual COGS SPEND increase ($480M×58% − ($480M/1.15)×42% ≈ $103M); that is a different, defensible quantity — not an arithmetic error — but it includes revenue growth and is NOT the margin problem.
Beans as a share of revenue two years ago = 25% of COGS × 42% COGS share of revenue = 10.5 points
Bean inflation's contribution to the COGS increase = 10.5 points × 40% = 4.2 points of revenue
Other inputs as points of revenue today = 31.5 points two years ago × 1.375 = 43.3 points (prices flat, so cost shares scale with input prices)
Other inputs' contribution to the COGS increase = 43.3 − 31.5 = 11.8 points of revenue

modelAnswerJsonb.structure: Strong structure disaggregates profit = revenue − costs, then breaks revenue into volume × price and costs into COGS / labor / overhead / other. The candidate should hypothesize which bucket is the driver before asking for data. Bonus: asks about competitive context (are peers also seeing this?) and pricing power.
modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
